## Problem 1


Suppose you have three multiple linear regression models that differ only in what explanatory variables
they include. The three models are:

- Model 1: $E(Y_i|A_i,B_i,C_i,D_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 A_i + \beta_2 B_i + \beta_3 C_i + \beta_4 D_i$;
- Model 2: $E(Y_i|A_i,B_i,C_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 A_i + \beta_2 B_i + \beta_3 C_i$; and
- Model 3: $E(Y_i|A_i,B_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 A_i + \beta_2 B_i$.

Please answer the following questions based on these three models.
Assume all four of our assumptions for linear regression are met for each model.


### Part (a) (4 points)

Suppose $D_3$ is missing in the data set, i.e., the third participant
is missing a value for the fourth explanatory variable.
There is no other missing data in the data set.
Which of the following metrics could you use to compare Model 1 and Model 2?
Select all that apply.


(i) $R^2$
(ii) $R_\text{adj}^2$
(iii) Likelihood
(iv) AIC


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

i and ii

Since these two models are fit on different observations, you can't use
likelihood-based methods to compare them.
Model 2 is fit on all $n$ observations and Model 1 is fit on $n - 1$ observations,
i.e., all the observations except the third.

This doesn't matter for $R^2$ because it's a ratio.
The contribution of the third observation is removed from both the numerator and denominator
of the $R^2$ for Model 1.
This also doesn't matter for $R^2_\text{adj}$ for similar reasons.

For a more thorough explanation: the key here is that Model 1 and Model 2 were fit using different datasets (Model 1 using $n - 1$ participants, Model 2 using all $n$ participants). Therefore, the likelihood of Model 2 is based on the distribution of the all of the observations, while the likelihood of Model 1 is based on the distribution of a subset of those observations. As a result, the two models aren't properly comparable using likelihood-based metrics, since those essentially rely on checking which model has a higher likelihood $\mathcal{L}$ based on the same distribution of observations. 

:::

### Part (b)

(4 points)
Suppose $D_3$ is missing in the data set, i.e., the third participant
is missing a value for the fourth explanatory variable.
There is no other missing data in the data set.
Which of the following metrics could you use to compare Model 2 and Model 3?
Select all that apply.


(i) $R^2$
(ii) $R_\text{adj}^2$
(iii) Likelihood
(iv) AIC


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

i, ii, iii, and iv

Since Models 2 and 3 don't use the fourth explanatory variable,
it doesn't matter if one of the observations is missing the fourth explanatory variable.
Both Models 2 and 3 can be fit on all $n$ observations.

:::

### Part (c)

(4 points)
Suppose $A_3$ is missing in the data set, i.e., the third participant
is missing a value for the first explanatory variable.
There is no other missing data in the data set.
Which of the following metrics could you use to compare Model 2 and Model 3?
Select all that apply.


(i) $R^2$
(ii) $R_\text{adj}^2$
(iii) Likelihood
(iv) AIC


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

i, ii, iii, and iv

Since both Models 2 and 3 use the first explanatory variable,
the third observation couldn't be used to fit either of them.
So, Models 2 and 3 will be fit on the same $n - 1$ observations.

:::

### Part (d)

(4 points)
Suppose you use a likelihood ratio test to compare Model 1 to Model 3.
You obtain a p-value of 0.00001.
What is a reasonable conclusion from this result?
Select all that apply.


(i)   Model 3 is at least as good as Model 1.
(ii)  Model 3 fits the data better than Model 1.
(iii) Model 2 is at least as good as Model 3.
(iv)  Model 1 fits the data better than Model 3.


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

iv

The null hypothesis is that the smaller model is the true model.
With such a low p-value, we would reject this hypothesis
and conclude that the larger model, Model 1,
fits the data better than the smaller model, Model 3.

:::
    
        

    
## Problem 2

(4 points)
If $X\sim\text{Poisson}(\mu)$ then $X$ could represent (select all that apply):

(a) A count.
(b) The time to an event.
(c) The outcome of a coin toss.
(d) Any decimal value.


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

(a)

The support of $X$ is $\{0,1,2,3,\dotsc\}$,
and a count is the only real world quantity in this list that matches that.

:::

## Problem 3

(4 points)
If $X\sim\text{Poisson}(\mu)$ then $\mu$ is (select all that apply):

(a) The standard deviation of $X$.
(b) The variance of $X$.
(c) The probability that $X = 1$.
(d) The mean of $X$.


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

(b) and (d)

:::

## Problem 4

(4 points)
Suppose you conduct quasi-Poisson regression and get an estimated dispersion parameter
of $\hat{\phi} = 100$.
This is evidence that (select all that apply):

(a) The mean is equal to the variance.
(b) The mean is not equal to the variance.
(c) The data are Poisson-distributed.
(d) The data are not Poisson-distributed.


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

(b) and (d)

With quasi-Poisson regression, we assume that $Var(Y) = \phi E(Y)$.
With the Poisson distribution, $Var(Y) = E(Y)$.
So, if $\phi$ is large, that's evidence that the data are not Poisson-distributed.

:::

## Problem 5

(1 point)
When there is overdispersion, we expect the standard errors
for quasi-Poisson regression to be \rule{1cm}{0.15mm}
the standard errors for Poisson regression.
(Select one.)

(a) the same as
(b) less than
(c) greater than


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

(c)

With more variability in the data, we expect lower precision in estimating our coefficients.

:::

## Problem 6

(1 point)
True or false:
R does not produce an AIC for quasi-Poisson regression because quasi-Poisson regression
does not use a likelihood.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

True

Quasi-Poisson regression doesn't correspond to an actual distribution.
It uses a quasi-likelihood instead of a likelihood.

:::

## Problem 7

(1 point)
True or false:
Assuming everything else stays the same (e.g., the data, the formula),
if you only change from Poisson to quasi-Poisson regression,
the estimates of the coefficients will not change.


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

True

:::

## Problem 8

(1 point)
True or false:
If $t_1 = t_2 = t_3 = \cdots = t_{n-1} = t_n = 1$
then we do not need to include an offset in Poisson regression.


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

True

$\log 1 = 0$

:::

## Problem 9

(1 point)
True or false:
It is appropriate to use the $R^2$ for model selection when only some of the
assumptions of linear regression are met.


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

True

The $R^2$ is just a function of the observed values, the fitted values,
and the average. It doesn't rely on any assumptions.

:::

## Problem 10

(1 point)
True or false:
It is appropriate to use the $R^2_\text{adj}$ for model selection when only some of the
assumptions of linear regression are met.


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

True

:::
